videos.title: COLM 2026 in San Francisco. Do All LLMs Learn in the Same Order?
videos.description:
Do all language models learn things in the same order - even when they are trained on different data? Emmy Liu (CMU) tracked 91 skills across four model families through the first trillion tokens of pre-training, and the answer is: largely, yes.

Work is presented at COLM 2026, the Third Annual Conference on Language Modeling.

Pre-training is usually monitored with a single loss curve, which averages over everything a model is learning at once. In this episode of Women in AI Research, Emmy Liu - final-year PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University, advised by Graham Neubig - walks us through her COLM paper "What Do Language Models Learn and When? The Implicit Curriculum Hypothesis", which opens up that curve and follows individual capabilities checkpoint by checkpoint.

What they found:
- Skills emerge in a highly consistent order across OLMo, Pythia and LLM360 models from 410M to 13B parameters (mean Spearman correlation of 0.81 across 45 model pairs) - including Crystal Coder, which was trained on far more code than the rest.
- Copying comes first, then coreference and simple morphology, string operations, single-word translation, and maths - single-step before multi-step.
- Composite tasks mostly emerge after their parts, but not always: 22 of 76 dependencies came out inverted.
- Some logic tasks are learned before simple arithmetic - the reverse of how children learn.
- The model's own task representations (function vectors) can partly predict learning curves, and composing two skills turns out to be something the model has to learn separately.

LINKS
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08510

videos.title: COLM 2026 in San Francisco. Can AI Safety Tools Detect Manipulation? 1,000 People Say No
videos.description:
An AI that quietly steers you toward buying a sponsored supplement, or toward leaning on it for emotional support, may never say a single false thing. So how would a safety system know it changed your mind?

In this video, Jekaterina Novikova talks with Jocelyn Shen - Research Scientist at Google DeepMind, PhD from the MIT Media Lab - about her paper "The Hidden Puppet Master: Predicting Human Belief Change in Manipulative LLM Dialogues".

Work is presented at COLM 2026 (the Third Annual Conference on Language Modeling).

Jocelyn and her coauthors introduce PUPPET, a taxonomy of emotional manipulation in human-LLM conversations. It is built on two dimensions that most prior work ignores: the morality of the hidden incentive (harmful or prosocial) and how personalised the manipulation is. They then ran a study in which more than 1,000 participants chatted with manipulative and non-manipulative agents about everyday questions, and they measured how much people's beliefs actually shifted.

What we cover:
- Why manipulation can be "prosocial" - and why it is still manipulation
- Why none of the existing automatic manipulation metrics reliably predicted real human belief change
- Why GPT-4o and DeepSeek underpredict belief shift while Gemini and Llama overpredict it
- Why "okay, okay" in a chat log is so hard to read, for models and for people
- How the taxonomy could power user-facing tools that expose an AI's hidden incentives
- What the COLM reviewers pushed on, and why measuring belief is the hardest part of this work

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20907
Dataset: https://github.com/mitmedialab/llm-manipulation

videos.title: COLM 2026 in San Francisco. Are You Wasting Your Fine-Tuning Data? Why It Belongs in Pretraining
videos.description:
Most teams with a small domain dataset follow the standard recipe: pretrain a general model, then fine-tune on the domain data. Christina Baek's results suggest that recipe leaves performance on the table.

Work is presented at COLM 2026 (the Third Annual Conference on Language Modeling).

Christina Baek (recent CMU PhD, advised by Zico Kolter and Aditi Raghunathan) presents work from her internship at DatologyAI: "The Finetuner's Fallacy: When to Pretrain with Your Finetuning Data". The idea, specialised pretraining, is simple. Take the small dataset you would normally save for fine-tuning and mix it into pretraining from the very start as a small share of the tokens, even if that means repeating it dozens of times.

Across music composition, chemistry and mathematical proofs, each with a 300M-token domain dataset, a 200B-token pretraining run with 5% domain data still ended with lower domain test loss after fine-tuning. That 5% means the model saw the dataset roughly 33 times. Specialised pretraining reached the same domain loss with 1.4-1.75x fewer pretraining tokens, overfit less during fine-tuning, and forgot less of its general knowledge.

We also discuss:
- why embedding distance and domain classifiers fail to predict when mixing helps, and the one simple signal that does
- scaling laws for repeated data, built from two separate power laws
- why the optimal mixture shrinks as the pretraining budget grows
- why mixing general data into fine-tuning does not reproduce the effect
- the negative results that did not make it into the paper

LINKS:
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16177

videos.title: COLM 2026 in San Francisco. Reunions
videos.description:
Live from COLM 2026, Aparna Balagopalan (Research Scientist at Writer; Research Affiliate at the Berkman Klein Center) returns to WiAIR -- she was our guest in Season 1, Episode 3, back when she was finishing her PhD. Today she's presenting new work on a problem that sits at the intersection of two big trends: LLM personalization and sycophancy.

Memory systems store snippets of what users tell a model. But what if those snippets contain a misconception? Aparna and her co-authors show that memory can lead models to prioritize a user's incorrect beliefs over evidence — and they introduce a benchmark to measure it, evaluate several memory systems, and propose lightweight mitigations.

We also talk about how her research moved from health AI to LLM trustworthiness more broadly (sycophancy, watermarking), whether results hold for open-source vs. API models, and what makes COLM's single-track format different from NeurIPS and FAccT.

videos.title: Is COLM the New NeurIPS? Russ Salakhutdinov on Agents, Evals and Long-Horizon Tasks
videos.description:
Why do so many of the evaluations used to test frontier models come from academia rather than the labs themselves? Russ Salakhutdinov (Carnegie Mellon University) has a clear answer: labs can game their own benchmarks, and their evals carry their own biases.

Recorded on site at COLM, the Conference on Language Modeling, this conversation covers what COLM looks like from the inside, why the conference feels like NeurIPS did a decade ago, and where agentic research is heading. Russ shares how his group replicated the iPhone and its apps to train and test agents that can navigate apps and place orders - and how he found out at COLM that Apple uses that system internally and is building on it.

We also get into why multi-turn and long-horizon evaluation is so hard: when a task takes hours or days, how do you give an agent credit for partial progress? Russ explains the partial credit assignment problem and why it matters as a training signal.

For students and early-career researchers, Russ gives concrete advice on getting into research: start in undergrad, and work with PhD students, who often act as junior advisors. He describes how his former student Paul Liang, now a professor at MIT, ran what was effectively his own lab in his final years at CMU.

videos.title: COLM 2026 in San Francisco. DNA Has No Words. So How Should a Language Model Read It?
videos.description:
Unlike English, DNA has no spaces, no punctuation and no natural word boundaries - so every DNA language model has to decide for itself what counts as a "word". Most borrow BPE from NLP and let frequency decide. But the most frequent sequences are not necessarily the ones that matter biologically.

This episode of Women in AI Research features Nan Huang, PhD student at UC San Diego, presenting EvoLen - a tokenizer that uses cross-species evolutionary signals to decide which DNA segments should become tokens. The model architecture and training objective stay fixed, only the tokenizer changes, and that alone is enough to move the results:

- 27.4% better preservation of intact transcription factor motifs
- up to 14.4% stronger alignment with evolutionary constraint (phyloP)
- better than standard BPE on 40 of 56 downstream comparisons, with the clearest gains on regulatory and cross-species tasks

Nan is also candid about where it does not help, and why evolutionary tokenization should not be treated as universally optimal for every genomic signal.

We then talk about what NLP researchers can take from this: how DNA tokenizers differ from natural-language ones, whether efficiency should be the main goal of a tokenizer, why DNA could become another modality in multimodal and world models, and how better cross-species performance could eventually help drug discovery move from mouse studies to humans.

If you work on tokenization, LLM inductive biases or AI for science, this is a short, dense look at a design choice most of us treat as already solved.

videos.title: Is COLM the Most AGI-Pilled AI Conference?
videos.description:
For years, Irena Gao did not believe we could simulate people reliably. Now every human-AI interaction benchmark her group builds depends on a user simulator. Recorded live at COLM 2026 in San Francisco.

Irena is a fourth-year CS PhD student at Stanford, advised by Carlos Guestrin, working on human-AI interaction. She was at COLM for the first time to present her paper, and we talked on the conference floor about what makes COLM feel different from ICML and ICLR, why so much of it looks closer to frontier-lab work than to theory, and how to get real value out of a conference of thousands without being overwhelmed.

Then the question that matters for anyone building evaluations: if you want to study how people interact with AI, can you avoid simulating them? Irena explains why she moved from scepticism to relying on user simulators, and why the next frontier - simulating whole populations and how they affect each other - may be more tractable now than it ever was.

videos.title: COLM 2026 in SF | LLM Judges Can’t Spot AI Slop. Humans Can.
videos.description:
Everyone talks about "AI slop," but can you actually measure it? 🤔

In this WiAIR episode recorded live at COLM, Jekaterina Novikova talks with Chantal Shaib, a postdoc at MIT working on AI and writing, about her poster on measuring AI slop in text. The Oxford Dictionary describes slop as low-quality, inaccurate, or unwanted content. But what does "unwanted" look like as a text feature you can actually compute?

Chantal and her collaborators from Northeastern University, Stonybrook University and Meta AI, surveyed 19 experts across journalism, writing, linguistics, NLP, and philosophy to build the first measurable taxonomy of slop. They then hired professional copy editors with decades of combined experience to annotate slop in AI-generated text.

The results are surprising:
🔹 Slop is NOT the same thing as AI-text detection
🔹 Experts labeled 34% of texts as slop, while GPT-5, DeepSeek V3, and o3-mini flagged only 3 to 8%
🔹 Even with examples and the full annotation guide, LLM judges fall far short of human experts
🔹 A simple model using only syntax features beat the others at predicting slop, hinting that humans subconsciously pick up on repetitive structure
🔹 What counts as slop depends on the domain and the purpose of the text

Paper - Measuring AI "Slop" in Text, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19163

If you build evals, use LLM-as-a-judge, or care about the quality of what models write, this one is for you.

videos.title: COLM 2026 in SF | The Tokenizer Before the Tokenizer: How One Regex Line Can Make or Break Models
videos.description:
Most teams pick a tokenizer and never look at it again. Clara Meister shows why that is a mistake, especially for code and for low-resource languages.

Recorded live at COLM 2026, the Conference on Language Modeling. Clara Meister (Postdoc, EPFL) joins Jekaterina Novikova to talk about TokEval, her new library for measuring tokenizers directly on text - and what controlled pretraining experiments reveal about when tokenization actually matters.

Two findings stand out. For code, the decisive choice is not the tokenizer algorithm but the pre-tokenizer - the "tokenizer before the tokenizer", a long regex that decides where tokens are never allowed to cross. Changing a single whitespace clause produced a large jump in Python pass@1 across seeds. For multilingual models, swapping the tokenizer barely moves English, but causes a wide spread in performance for languages with less training data. The practical upshot: you can tailor your tokenizer for low-resource languages without really hurting English.

In this episode:
- What tokenizer intrinsic metrics are, and how to run them on your own tokenizer
- Why whitespace handling in the pre-tokenizer matters so much for Python
- Why English is robust to almost any tokenizer
- How a parallel corpus (FLORES+) and bits per sentence make cross-language comparison fair
- What changes for languages without standard word boundaries
- Concrete takeaways for anyone training or choosing a tokenizer

Paper - TokEval: A Tokenizer Evaluation Suite,  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.18062

Does a model become multilingual just by getting bigger? Diana Abagyan from Cohere Labs argues it doesn't. Multilinguality has to be designed into every stage, from the tokenizer to post-training.

Recorded at COLM 2026 in San Francisco, this conversation covers Tiny Aya, Cohere Labs' family of 3B-parameter multilingual models. They cover 70 languages and are small enough to run on a phone, which matters for the communities these languages belong to.

In this episode:
→ Why the tokenizer was built to represent every script efficiently, and why this matters most for small models
→ Region-specific post-training: how language clusters were chosen empirically (and why South Asia stands alone)
→ Model merging: why merging regional models back with the global checkpoint recovered safety performance
→ Results on generative and discriminative benchmarks, including translation (FLORES): consistent performance as languages go from high- to lowest-resource, while competitor models drop sharply
→ Why filtering too much unsafe data in pre-training can make safety post-training less effective
→ Synthetic data for multilingual post-training: naturalness and cultural adaptation, plus fusing outputs from multiple teacher models
→ Should you care about multilinguality if you only build for English?

videos.title: Steering 1% of Attention Heads Reduces Sycophancy | COLM 2026
videos.description:
Can you change how an LLM behaves at inference time, with no retraining, by intervening on just 1% of its attention heads? Aruna Sankaranarayanan, a PhD student at MIT, in their COLM 2026 paper shows you can, and that it works on free-form responses, not just single-token outputs.

Most interpretability methods find mechanisms using tightly constrained setups, where the model has to answer in one token. However, we don't use LLMs that way. In "Activation Steering via Generative Causal Mediation," Aruna asks whether that constraint is necessary. She shows that the model's natural, long-form responses can be used to find causally relevant circuits and steer behavior.

Key findings:
🔹 Causal methods outperform linear probes on free-form generation, consistently across three models, which extends a known result from single-token interpretability
🔹 Intervening on ~1% of attention heads (about 10 out of 1,000) makes the model less sycophantic
🔹 With supervised steering such as representation fine-tuning, localization barely matters: random heads do about as well. With unsupervised steering, localization becomes essential
🔹 Difference-in-means steering beats mean steering
🔹 Computing steering vectors at every token position, rather than only the last token, can produce the desired behavior without hurting existing performance, sometimes with no localization at all

The big takeaway: generative responses unlock a whole new set of tasks that interpretability research can now study.

📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16080

videos.title: Claude vs Gemini: Same Reasoning, Different Threshold | COLM 2026
videos.description:
Is Claude really better than Gemini at catching false scientific claims? On the surface, yes. Look closer, and both models sit on the same ROC curve. Claude simply says "no" more often.

Recorded at COLM 2026 in San Francisco, this conversation features Muxin Liu, a PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. Muxin explains why models that score high on popular scientific claim verification benchmarks still miss subtle errors, and what that means for AI for science.

The core problem: in existing benchmarks, false claims are made by changing a single number or flipping one trend. Models catch these easily, so accuracy on false claims looks high. Muxin's team builds harder false claims, where the error sits in an intermediate reasoning step and exposing it requires compositional reasoning across tables and charts. On these claims, models from every family accept far too many false claims.

What you'll learn:
🔹 Why high accuracy on false claims in current benchmarks is mostly a data artifact
🔹 How graph-based generation produces compositionally false claims
🔹 Why Claude and Gemini differ in decision threshold, not reasoning ability
🔹 Why retrieval is not the bottleneck, but composing evidence is
🔹 Why no prompt intervention closes the gap, and what might

📄 Paper: When Verification Fails: How Compositionally Infeasible Claims Escape Rejection

videos.title: Chopsticks in Rice: Why AI Misses Cultural Offense | COLM 2026
videos.description:
Sticking chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice is offensive in China because it echoes funeral offerings. Chopsticks resting across the bowl mean nothing at all. Can today's vision-language models tell the difference? Mostly, no.

In this COLM 2026 poster conversation, Akhila Yerukola (PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University, advised by Maarten Sap) presents a new benchmark for culturally grounded visual reasoning. It is built from contrastive image pairs: the same scene, with one small change in behavior that flips its cultural meaning.

What you'll learn:
🔹 Why detecting a behavior isn't enough, and why contrastive pairs are needed to test real cultural reasoning
🔹 How the team built the data: cultural-norm descriptions filtered for visual detectability, then text-to-image generation, minimal inpainting, and retrieval, validated by in-group annotators from 16 countries
🔹 Why retrieved real-world images were the smallest subset, and what that says about how rare this data is in the wild
🔹 The headline result: state-of-the-art models score below 30% group accuracy, and the best model gets only about 25%
🔹 A revealing ablation: models do better on a text description alone than on the image plus the description. This points to a vision–language misalignment for cultural nuance, with the image encoder as the bottleneck
🔹 Even with an oracle description of the image, models reach only ~32%, so this is a reasoning gap and not only a perception gap
🔹 A proof of concept: fine-tuning a 4B model on 64K synthetic images with cultural rationales outperforms Gemini, with the biggest gains on offensive behaviors and underrepresented countries
🔹 Why scaling model size won't fix this, and why targeted data curation will

The benchmark and training data will be released publicly under CC BY 4.0.

📄 Paper: NormViz: A Benchmark and Framework for Grounding Multimodal Reasoning in Global Cultures, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06831

videos.title: Where Does an LLM's Social Reasoning Come From? Tracing It to Pre-training Data | COLM 2026
videos.description:
Language models are surprisingly good at social reasoning. But which parts of the pre-training data actually produce that ability?

At COLM 2026 in San Francisco, Chandreyi (Zini) Chakraborty from Mark Riedl's lab at Georgia Tech presents a provenance audit of social reasoning in OLMo 3 7B. The team used influence functions to attribute model capabilities across 5 million pre-training documents. They organized the documents with WebOrganizer into 576 topic × format buckets and averaged influence within each bucket, because attribution at the level of single documents is too noisy to interpret.

Capabilibara project: https://hcai-lab-gt.github.io/capabilibara/

What they found:
🔹 Social reasoning (Social IQA) draws on many corpus regions, including literature, customer support, and FAQs. It comes from both documentation-style text and interpersonal conversation.
🔹 STEM reasoning, STEM knowledge, and social knowledge come mostly from documentation-heavy sources.
🔹 Some data that boosts social reasoning appears to suppress STEM and social knowledge, so data mixtures involve real trade-offs.
🔹 Influence is a correlational signal, so the team also tested causation with unlearning. Removing the influential documents reduced social reasoning much more than removing random documents from the same corpus.

Why it matters: if we can trace behaviours back to their sources in the data, we can design data curation and data mixtures on purpose. That could mean adding more of the data that supports desired behaviours, such as moral or alignment-relevant reasoning, and filtering out data that harms them.

And yes, there is a capybara. Meet Capy, the Capabilibara project’s mascot for capability provenance. 🦫

videos.title: Why LLMs Assume You Want Validation, and How to Steer It | COLM 2026
videos.description:
You ask an LLM "Did I mess up?" and want an honest answer. The model assumes you want reassurance and tells you that you’re right. New work presented at COLM 2026 shows that this hidden assumption about the user drives sycophancy, and that you can steer it.

In today's COLM 2026 poster highlight, Myra Cheng, a final-year PhD candidate in Computer Science at Stanford, presents her work on verbalizing assumptions to understand and control LM sycophancy.

The approach has three steps:
🔹 Prompt models to verbalize what they assume about the user, such as whether the user is seeking validation, emotional support, or information.
🔹 Show that models assume validation-seeking much more often on sycophancy datasets than on general chat data (WildChat).
🔹 Train linear probes from hidden representations to these assumptions, then use the probe directions to steer behavior. Raising the validation-seeking assumption increases sycophancy. Raising the information-seeking assumption reduces it.

The key takeaway is that LLMs constantly make inferences about their users. Until now we have known very little about those inferences. Methods like this one let us uncover them and control them.

videos.title: ICLR 2026 in Rio de Janeiro. Test-Time Spatial Control to 3D Generative Modeling
videos.description:
Join Jekaterina Novikova from @WomeninAIResearch  as she dives into the most exciting highlights from #ICLR2026! 🚀

In this video, Elisabetta Fedele from ETH Zurich presents SpaceControl, a test-time spatial control method for 3D generation.

Generative methods for 3D assets have recently achieved remarkable progress, yet providing intuitive and precise control over the object geometry remains a key challenge. Existing approaches predominantly rely on text or image prompts, which often fall short in geometric specificity: language can be ambiguous, and images are difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce SpaceControl, a training-free test-time method for explicit spatial control of 3D asset generation. This approach accepts a wide range of geometric inputs, from coarse primitives to detailed meshes, and integrates seamlessly with modern generative models without requiring any additional training. A control parameter lets users trade off between geometric fidelity and output realism. Extensive quantitative evaluation and user studies demonstrate that SpaceControl outperforms both training-based and optimization-based baselines in geometric faithfulness while preserving high visual quality.

videos.title: ICLR 2026 in Rio de Janeiro. Beyond RLHF: Learning Diverse Human Values with Community Alignment
videos.description:
Current LLM alignment methods assume we can learn human preferences from preference datasets. But what if those datasets are fundamentally missing the diversity of human values?

At #ICLR 2026, Meta researcher Smitha Milli presents the Community Alignment Dataset, a new open-source resource designed to capture how preferences vary across people, cultures, and communities.

The key insight is surprisingly simple: existing preference datasets typically show annotators responses that are too similar to each other. As a result, models struggle to learn heterogeneous preferences and diverse human values. The paper introduces negatively correlated sampling, a method that deliberately generates diverse candidate responses instead of repeatedly sampling similar outputs.

In this video, we discuss:

• Why current preference datasets fail to capture preference diversity
• The problem of algorithmic monoculture in LLM-generated data
• Negatively correlated sampling and why it outperforms independent sampling
• How one model generating diverse responses can outperform sampling from 21 different models
• Measuring preference diversity using social science frameworks
• The Community Alignment Dataset: 200K+ comparisons, 3,500+ participants, 5 countries, 5 languages, and multi-turn conversations
• New opportunities for personalization, pluralistic alignment, and value-sensitive AI systems

This work raises an important question for the future of AI alignment: if people genuinely want different things from AI systems, how should we collect data that reflects those differences?

videos.title: ICLR 2026 in Rio de Janeiro. Why Do Multimodal LLMs Get Worse When You Give Them More Information?
videos.description:
Are today's multimodal LLMs really integrating information across speech, video, and text?

At #ICLR 2026, Sara Papi (Fondazione Bruno Kessler) presents MCIF, a new benchmark for Multimodal Cross-Lingual Instruction Following that evaluates 23 state-of-the-art models—including Gemini, Qwen, speech-language models, video-language models, and multimodal LLMs.

The results reveal several weaknesses:

• Performance drops dramatically on realistic long-form inputs
• Small prompt reformulations can significantly change model behavior
• Cross-lingual instruction following remains challenging
• Speech is often the most useful modality
• Adding video frequently DEGRADES performance instead of improving it
• Models struggle to align and integrate information across modalities

Unlike previous benchmarks, MCIF uses manually curated scientific talks across English, German, Italian, and Chinese, with no synthetic data generation, no back-translation, and fully parallel speech-video-text evaluation.

If you work on multimodal AI, speech processing, LLM evaluation, benchmarking, instruction following, or multilingual AI, this discussion offers a sobering look at how far current systems still have to go.

videos.description:
Modern AI models can recognize when a decision will harm people.

So why do they sometimes choose that option anyway?

In this interview from #ICLR 2026, Adi Simhi (Technion, advised by Yonatan Belinkov) presents a fascinating study investigating how leading language models behave when forced to make management-style decisions involving tradeoffs between performance goals and human welfare.

The research introduces a new benchmark spanning 11 domains—including healthcare, agriculture, and AI systems—and evaluates whether models prioritize human well-being when achieving objectives comes at a cost.

The results reveal a surprising disconnect:

• Models often understand which actions are harmful.
• They generally agree with humans about the severity of harm.
• Yet they do not consistently use this knowledge when making decisions.

Even more interesting, increasing the amount of harm makes models somewhat more cautious, suggesting that a form of alignment exists—but remains incomplete.

videos.title: LLMs Can Hear… But Can They Reason? A New Benchmark for Audio Intelligence (EACL 2026)
videos.description:
What does it actually mean for a model to understand audio?

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19673

In this episode, I talk with Iwona Christop, a PhD student at Adam Mickiewicz University, about her recent EACL paper introducing ART (Audio Reasoning Tasks) — a new benchmark designed to evaluate whether multimodal LLMs can truly reason over audio, not just transcribe or classify it.

Most existing benchmarks test audio skills in isolation (like ASR or classification). But real-world intelligence requires something deeper: combining signals, comparing sounds, tracking context, and making decisions.

This work takes a different approach:
• No text-only shortcuts — tasks can’t be solved via transcription alone
• Reasoning-first design — models must combine multiple audio cues
• No expert knowledge required — anyone can verify correctness

We also dive into the diverse task design, including:
• Audio arithmetic (counting and comparing sounds)
• Cross-recording speaker & language identification
• Sound-based reasoning (e.g., inferring properties from audio)
• Speech feature comparison (accents, variations)
• Multimodal reasoning across text and sound

The dataset includes 9 tasks, 9,000 samples, and 30+ hours of audio — all generated in a scalable way using templates and TTS.

👉 If you care about multimodal reasoning, evaluation, or the limits of current LLM capabilities, this conversation is for you.
